Gustav Vasa
gūs'tahv vah'sa
n. (Gustav I Vasa, 1496–1560, king of Sweden, under whom the realm left the Roman obedience)
Swedish Gustav, from Norse elements meaning staff of the Goths; Vasa, a sheaf, from the family arms.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Gustav Vasa led the rising that expelled the Danes in 1521, was elected king in 1523, and held Sweden for thirty-seven years. He is the sovereign under whom the Swedish Reformation was carried, and the dictionary states his part without flattery. He protected Olaus Petri when the bishops wanted him silenced, allowed and funded the Swedish New Testament of 1526 and the whole Bible of 1541, and carried the Diet of Västerås in 1527, which put the church of the realm under the crown. He also stripped that church with a thoroughness that shocked the very preachers who had argued his case, took the bells and the plate, reduced the bishops to pensioners, and in 1539 had Olaus Petri and Laurentius Andreae condemned to death for resisting him. A king may be the means of a reformation without being a reformed man, and Scripture itself keeps the two questions apart. “All the ways of a man are clean in his own eyes; but the LORD weigheth the spirits” (Pro 16:2).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines confiscation as the act of condemning private property to public use, and a nursing father as a protector who cherishes.

expand to see more

CONFISCA'TION, n. The act of condemning as forfeited, and adjudging to the public treasury.

NUR'SING FATHER, One who nourishes and protects, as a prince who fosters the church.

SOV'EREIGN, n. A supreme lord or ruler; one who possesses the highest authority without control.

MO'TIVE, n. That which incites to action; that which determines the choice of the will.

Key Scripture

Pro 16:2 — "All the ways of a man are clean in his own eyes; but the LORD weigheth the spirits."

Isa 49:23 — "And kings shall be thy nursing fathers, and their queens thy nursing mothers: they shall bow down to thee with their face toward the earth, and lick up the dust of thy feet; and thou shalt know that I am the LORD: for they shall not be ashamed that wait for me."

2Ch 34:31 — "And the king stood in his place, and made a covenant before the LORD, to walk after the LORD, and to keep his commandments, and his testimonies, and his statutes, with all his heart, and with all his soul, to perform the words of the covenant which are written in this book."

Jer 17:5 — "Thus saith the LORD; Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm, and whose heart departeth from the LORD."

Modern Corruption

The king who gave Sweden a Bible and took the church's bells.

expand to see more

Gustav Vasa is the standing exhibit for the claim that the Reformation was politics in a cassock: a prince wanting the church's revenues found a doctrine that let him take them. The dictionary grants the fact and denies the inference. The confiscations were real and indefensible, and the preachers said so at the cost of a capital sentence; that is precisely why the doctrine cannot be reduced to the policy. A gospel invented to serve a king does not produce men who go to trial against him.

The principle to recover is that God uses magistrates without endorsing them, and that the promise of royal protection in Isaiah — “And kings shall be thy nursing fathers, and their queens thy nursing mothers” (Isa 49:23) — is a promise about God's provision and not a licence for the nursing father. Jeremiah supplies the balance the Swedish church learned the hard way: “Cursed be the man that trusteth in man, and maketh flesh his arm” (Jer 17:5).

Usage

"“but the LORD weigheth the spirits” (Pro 16:2) — a reforming king with mixed motives."

"“kings shall be thy nursing fathers” (Isa 49:23) — the promise he partly fulfilled."

"“Cursed be the man that trusteth in man” (Jer 17:5) — what the Swedish preachers learned by 1539."
